title: Wise Words
subtitle: WITH MARCO REYES  ·  STORY NIGHT

segments.head: TONIGHT: LACEY'S BIG CALL
segments.author: Wise Words
lines: Good evening, everyone.
I'm Marco Reyes, and this is Wise Words.
Tonight's story is about Lacey Doyle, a mail sorter from Eugene, Oregon.
Her old pickup needed a new transmission, so she became a weekend softball umpire.
Thirty dollars a game. Plus all the yelling you can eat.

segments.head: CHAPTER 1: THE BOOS
segments.quote: It is not the critic who counts.
segments.author: Theodore Roosevelt
lines: Her first game, a man in the bleachers yelled, Get some glasses, lady!
That night, she almost quit.
Then she saw a dugout poster from Theodore Roosevelt:
It is not the critic who counts.
He had a hot dog. She had a job. She came back Saturday.

segments.head: CHAPTER 2: BIG RICK
segments.quote: Anger is never without a reason, but seldom with a good one.
segments.author: Benjamin Franklin
lines: Then came Big Rick, coach of the Lumberjacks, a man shaped like a refrigerator.
He stormed out over a strike, nose to nose, red as a fire truck.
Lacey felt her temper rise. Then she heard Grandpa's favorite line, from Ben Franklin:
Anger is never without a reason, but seldom with a good one.
She stepped back and said calmly, Coach, it was a strike. Play ball.

segments.head: CHAPTER 3: THE BLOWN CALL
segments.quote: A man should never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong.
segments.author: Alexander Pope
lines: Two weeks later, she called a runner out at second.
A player showed her the video. He was safe by a mile.
She wanted to hide behind her mask. Then she remembered Alexander Pope, the English writer:
A man should never be ashamed to own he has been in the wrong.
Next game, she told both teams, I blew that one. Nobody booed. One guy clapped.

segments.head: CHAPTER 4: TWO EARS
segments.quote: We have two ears and one mouth, so we should listen more than we say.
segments.author: Zeno of Citium
lines: Still, every argument became a shouting match.
Her partner Walt, a retired umpire, shared a line from Zeno, an old Greek thinker:
We have two ears and one mouth, so we should listen more than we say.
So Lacey let the coaches talk first. Then she explained the rule in ten words.
Some arguments even ended in a laugh.

segments.head: CHAPTER 5: THE TAG
segments.quote: To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage.
segments.author: Confucius
lines: Championship night. Lumberjacks down by one, runner sliding home.
The tag beat him by half an inch. The whole crowd wanted safe.
For one second, she thought, let it go. Then she thought of Confucius, the Chinese teacher:
To see what is right and not to do it is want of courage.
Out! The Lumberjacks lost. The bleachers were not happy.

segments.head: CHAPTER 6: THE LEMONADE
segments.quote: I never did a day's work in my life. It was all fun.
segments.author: Thomas Edison
lines: Afterward, Big Rick walked over. Lacey braced for round two.
Instead, he handed her a lemonade. Right call. I hated it. Do our games next year.
Somebody asked why she does this for thirty bucks.
She grinned and quoted the inventor Thomas Edison:
I never did a day's work in my life. It was all fun.

segments.head: THAT'S TONIGHT'S STORY
segments.quote: Ignore the hecklers. Stay cool. Own it. Listen first. Make the call. Have fun.
segments.author: Marco Reyes
lines: That's tonight's story.
Ignore the hecklers. Stay cool. Own your mistakes. Listen first. Make the call. Have fun.
I umpired a family softball game once. My own sister threw me out.
I'm Marco Reyes. Good night.
